root.note: English park comes from French parc; English made the verb to park, ‘to put in a park’.

history: In France you leave your car au parking, and English speakers are puzzled: in English, parking is what you do, while the place is a car park or a parking lot. The TLFi explains it: French probably shortened American phrases like parking lot or parking place. The French word is first recorded in 1926 for a place to leave vehicles; the sense ‘the act of parking’ only follows in 1953. English parking itself comes from to park, ‘to put in a park’, and park is French parc. So the word went out as parc and came back as parking, losing its second half on the way. In 1959 a committee for French technical terms proposed parc instead, but le parking won. Grammar: stationner is ‘to park’.
historyEinfach: Parking is an English word, but French uses it in its own way. Le parking is the place where you leave your car: a car park. English park comes from French parc. So the word went to English and came back to French.

elsewhere.text: Careful in English: say car park (UK) or parking lot (US) for the place. French le parking is a pseudo-anglicism.
